name: reference-monitor
intent: Confine every access decision to one small, always-invoked component that the code it polices can neither reach nor replace, so that the protection is tamperproof and its completeness can be argued and tested instead of assumed.
problem: A protected operation must be unbypassable, but the check lives in the same code, the same address space or the same privilege domain as the code it is supposed to constrain: a dependency, plugin, administrative path or maintenance tool can skip, replace or reconfigure it, and nothing demonstrates that all paths were covered.
context: Systems in which a resource or operation is reachable from more than one code path and the code under confinement is not fully trusted: operating-system kernels and hypervisors, sandboxes that run untrusted code, multi-tenant platforms and plugin hosts, regulated systems that must show evidence of complete protection, and device firmware. The pattern presupposes an identity for every subject, a policy source the monitor can read, and an isolation primitive to put the monitor behind - a kernel or LSM hook, a hypervisor, a privilege-separated process, a container or an OS sandbox.
benefits: Unbypassability becomes structural rather than a matter of discipline: one component stands between every subject and the protected objects, so the question whether a path can reach the resource without passing the monitor has a single answer that can be enumerated.
Verifiability: because the mechanism is small and self-contained it can be tested exhaustively, reviewed line by line, modelled and even proved, and that evidence can be reproduced for every release.

Tamper resistance: the monitor is structured to be out of reach of the code it polices - a separate privilege domain, a kernel hook, a sandbox or a hypervisor - instead of being a library the caller may replace or patch.

Consistency: interactive, batch, administrative and recovery paths all meet the same decision, so the same rules apply to every caller and policy changes or revocations take effect on the next decision.
Audit and forensics: every decision, granted or denied, passes a single place that can log, meter and alarm, which is what makes an access record trustworthy to an assessor.

Independent testability: the monitor can be exercised against its own table of subjects, operations and objects, including missing-identity and unreachable-policy cases, without standing up the resources it protects.
tradeoffs: Verification is the price of the guarantee: the protection is only as good as the argument that the mechanism is complete and correct, so keeping it small means refusing features, and every later addition re-opens the analysis that justified the design.

The monitor is a single point of failure and of policy churn: a bug in it is a total bypass, its fail-closed behaviour must be tested for every error path, and it is the component an attacker studies first.

Tamper resistance is a deployment property, not a code property: in managed and dynamic runtimes reflection, agents, loaders and monkey patching all defeat in-process enforcement, so the pattern usually forces a process, container, kernel or hypervisor boundary with its performance and operational cost.

A monitor at the wrong layer creates gaps: if it mediates an API but not the resource itself (raw descriptors, paths, pointers, connections, shared memory), code simply goes around it, so the interface it controls must actually be the only route in.

It guarantees the enforcement, not the policy: a monitor that decides faithfully with the wrong rules, or that fails open on error, is worse than a visible absence of protection, and the rules live outside the small core and therefore outside its assurance.

Per-access mediation costs latency in hot paths (per request, per syscall, per object access), which constrains where the monitor can sit and pushes toward coarse decisions that are easier to satisfy but less precise.

participants.responsibility: The active entity whose access is decided - a user, process, thread, tenant or service - identified by credentials, a principal or a capability the monitor can verify without the subject's cooperation.

The small, always-invoked component that resolves the subject, consults the policy and permits or denies the operation. It holds no business state, performs the mediated operation itself, and is placed where the code it polices cannot modify or disable it.

The replaceable authority that holds the rules and attributes the monitor reads - an access control list, a capability table, a policy decision point, a kernel rule set. It is intentionally outside the verified core so that rules can change without invalidating the verification.
The resource or operation the monitor mediates access to; it is reachable only through the monitor, never through references handed to callers before or after a decision.

The isolation that makes the monitor tamperproof - the privilege domain, kernel or LSM hook, hypervisor, container or sandbox the monitor runs in, together with everything inside it and the list of what it assumes about the outside.

The enumeration of mediated operations plus the test suite, analyses or proof whose completeness can be assured; it is what turns always invoked and tamperproof from intentions into a claim a reviewer can check.

use_cases: Operating-system kernels and hypervisors: the TCB layer that every syscall or hypercall passes through, deciding access to files, memory and devices while the rules live outside the small mechanism.

Sandboxing untrusted code: seccomp-BPF allow-lists, Landlock rulesets and container or OS security profiles, which mediate from outside the sandboxed program so that it cannot widen its own permissions.

Multi-tenant platforms: one admission and enforcement component (API gateway, service-mesh sidecar, framework authorization filter) through which every request for a tenant resource passes, with its own test suite and a per-release assurance statement.

Regulated systems: payment, medical and avionics platforms where the protection must be demonstrably complete, so the monitor and its evidence are the artifact a reviewer or assessor examines, separately from the application.
Desktop and mobile app sandboxes: entitlements and the operating system's sandbox limit what an application may reach, independently of what the application's own code checks.
Embedded and device firmware: a minimal policy kernel or memory-protection configuration decides which task may touch which memory-mapped region, with the mechanism small enough to inspect.

Linux seccomp-BPF: the kernel evaluates a per-process filter for each system call and applies an allow, deny, trap or kill action; use it as the kernel-side mediation layer while policy construction remains outside the protected kernel mechanism.

Android Application Sandbox: AOSP gives each app a distinct Linux UID and combines kernel-enforced DAC with SELinux isolation, so the operating system rather than app code mediates access to other apps and protected resources.

Kubernetes Pod Security Admission: the built-in apiserver admission controller evaluates Pod creation against baseline or restricted standards with explicit exemptions and audit or warn modes; treat this as admission mediation and pair it with runtime isolation for complete protection.
avoid_when: The requirement is business authorization among trusted code: a policy object with a guard (policy-guard, complete-mediation) is cheaper and clearer than building a trusted computing base with verification evidence.

No isolation primitive is available and none can be obtained: then the honest answer is to use the platform's boundary (container, OS sandbox, native code, separate process) rather than claim tamper resistance for an in-process function.
The monitor would have to absorb business rules or grow with the application: a large monitor cannot be verified, so keep the decision core tiny and move the rules into a replaceable policy source.

The resource is already completely mediated below you (kernel LSM, database row-level security, managed identity gateway, container runtime): configure that mechanism instead of stacking a second, disagreeing one on top.
The protected operations are not reachable through one controllable interface (the code shares memory and calls arbitrary functions): isolate first, otherwise completeness cannot even be stated.

The access is a tight inner loop over data that has already been confined and cannot change owner: decide once at the boundary and hand the loop an immutable view rather than paying a monitor call per iteration.
anti_patterns: In-process monitor in the same trust domain as the code it constrains, described as tamperproof - a library call that any dependency may bypass, patch or replace, especially where reflection, loader hooks or agents exist.
A monitor that can be switched off by the code it polices: a runtime flag, a mutable policy object handed out to callers, an administrative bypass endpoint or a debug mode that skips the decision.
Mediating the API instead of the resource: handing out descriptors, paths, pointers, connections or mutable copies after a permitted decision, so the next access never reaches the monitor.
A monitor grown into a policy engine or a domain service: it now holds rules, I/O and business logic, so it is no longer small enough to verify and its review becomes a review of the application.
A monitor without verification: no enumeration of mediated operations, no isolated test suite, no bypass tests - the completeness claim then rests on intent instead of evidence.
Fail-open error handling: a missing identity, an unreachable policy or an internal exception treated as permission.
design_principles: Economy of mechanism: the smallest mechanism that can decide and enforce is the one that can be verified; every feature added inside the monitor is subtracted from the assurance argument.
Complete mediation: every access to every object is checked, including initialisation, recovery, maintenance and administrative paths.
Fail-safe defaults: when the monitor cannot decide - no identity, no policy, internal error - the access is denied.
Separation of policy from mechanism: rules live in a replaceable source; only the decision and enforcement core belongs to the verified boundary.

Least privilege and least common mechanism: the monitor holds only the rights it needs to decide and perform the mediated operation, and shares as little mechanism as possible with the code it polices.
Open design and independent verification: protection must survive publication of the design, and completeness must be demonstrable by analysis and tests rather than asserted.
best_practices: Draw the trust boundary before writing code: write down what the monitor may assume and what must hold outside it, and keep the list of components inside the boundary short.
Keep the monitor to a single responsibility and a small interface; enumerate every mediated operation and treat a new operation as a change to that enumeration and to its tests.

Place the monitor where the code under mediation cannot edit it - kernel or LSM hook, hypervisor, privilege-separated process, container or OS sandbox - and state plainly when the enforcement is only advisory.

Decide and perform in one operation (a syscall with resolve constraints, a check inside the guarded call) so that no check-then-use window exists, and never hand out a raw reference after a granted decision.

Give the monitor its own test suite: table-driven decisions, fault injection for missing identity and unreachable policy, and bypass tests that try to reach the protected object around it; keep the evidence with the release.
Deny by default and record every denial; fail closed on error and alert when identity or policy cannot be obtained.
Review the monitor as the security boundary it is, separately from feature work, and re-run the verification argument whenever the core, its interface or its placement changes.
sources: NIST CSRC glossary, "reference monitor": a set of design requirements on a reference validation mechanism that, as a key component of an operating system, enforces an access control policy over all subjects and objects - always invoked (complete mediation), tamperproof, and small enough to be subject to analysis and tests whose completeness can be assured (verifiable).
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations (2020) - the definition source the glossary entry cites.

Anderson, J. P., Computer Security Technology Planning Study, ESD-TR-73-51, USAF Electronic Systems Division (1972) - origin of the reference monitor concept and of the term reference validation mechanism.

DoD 5200.28-STD, Trusted Computer System Evaluation Criteria (1985) - turns the concept into an evaluation requirement: the TCB implements a reference monitor that is tamperproof, always invoked and small enough to be analysed and tested.

Schumacher, Fernandez-Buglioni, Hybertson, Buschmann & Sommerlad, Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering, Wiley 2006 - the security-patterns canon whose vocabulary (policy, guard, protected system, enforcement) this catalog family belongs to.
